options.rationale: The aim is right but the method publicly embarrasses the lead before he has had any chance to explain, which hardens a conflict that a private word might resolve. Speed is not the issue here; the record can wait a month.

questions.explanation: Conflicts over credit are about recognition, and they damage collaboration quickly because the person overlooked stops sharing. Where the project manager controls the channel in which recognition is given, such as reports, minutes or packs, the record can be put right there without escalation. The behaviour is best addressed privately with the person concerned first, because it allows for honest error and avoids turning a correction into a public contest.
questions.mindset: Use the channels you own to put the record right, and deal with the behaviour face to face.

questions.stem: On a new secondary school building, the structural engineer and the architect have argued at the last three design meetings about the sports hall roof: long-span steel trusses or a glulam timber frame. Both bring cost data and fire assessments, and each round has produced a better option than the last. The sponsor tells you the bickering is unprofessional and asks you to stop it. Design freeze is six weeks away. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask both of them to keep the disagreement out of the full design meetings and settle the roof question between themselves in a separate session.
options.rationale: This does what the sponsor asked, which is its appeal. But it moves a debate that is improving the design out of the forum where others can test it, and leaves it with no deadline, so it may end in stalemate or a private deal.

options.text: Explain to the sponsor that the debate is improving the design, and agree a decision date and criteria so that it reaches a conclusion before the freeze.
options.rationale: The premise of the sponsor's request is wrong: this is productive task conflict, and each round has produced a better option. The project manager's job is to protect it while bounding it, and a date and criteria ensure it converges in time.

options.text: Review both options yourself against the budget and the fire strategy, and make the decision now so that the design meetings can move on.
options.rationale: Taking the decision ends the noise, but it cuts off a debate that is still producing better options, six weeks before it needs to end. A candidate picking this treats the existence of the conflict as the problem.

options.text: Remind both of them of the team's agreed meeting behaviours, and ask them to present their cost and fire evidence more calmly and concisely at the next design meeting.
options.rationale: This treats a disagreement about substance as a conduct problem, though the stem describes evidence-based argument, not misconduct. Asking for calm can chill exactly the challenge that has been improving the roof design.

questions.explanation: Conflict over the substance of the work, argued with evidence, is one of the main ways a team reaches a better answer. The project manager's job is to keep it focused on the task and bounded in time, not to suppress it because it looks uncomfortable to people watching. Whether a conflict needs to stop depends on what it is producing and whether it is turning personal, not on how heated it sounds.
questions.mindset: Judge a conflict by what it is producing, not by how it sounds.

questions.stem: You are leading a hybrid warehouse-system rollout for a Belgian distributor. The software supplier's account manager and your procurement lead are in a bitter dispute over a €6,000 invoice for extra training days that procurement says were never ordered. The supplier's support responses have slowed noticeably, and cut-over is in nine days. You hold a €20,000 contingency to spend at your discretion, and the contract allows invoices to be paid under protest. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Authorise payment of the €6,000 under protest from contingency, so the cut-over support is protected, and settle the entitlement question after go-live.
options.rationale: This is a deliberate trade: a small, recoverable sum in exchange for removing friction from the riskiest nine days of the project. Paying under protest preserves the right to recover the money, and the decision is within the project manager's own authority.

options.text: Back your procurement lead and tell the account manager that the invoice will not be paid until a signed order for the training days is produced.
options.rationale: Procurement may well be right on entitlement, which makes this feel principled. But it stakes a nine-day cut-over on winning a €6,000 argument, and a candidate choosing it has not weighed the size of the issue against the size of the risk.

options.text: Escalate the dispute to the supplier's account director and your own procurement director, asking them jointly to resolve the invoice before the cut-over date.
options.rationale: Escalation is a reasonable route for a commercial dispute, but with nine days left it adds time and uncertainty, and it passes up an authority the project manager already holds to remove the problem today.

options.text: Raise the slower support responses with the account manager as a separate service-level issue, keeping that apart from the invoice dispute.
options.rationale: Separating the two issues is good negotiating practice in principle. In practice the supplier has already linked them, and a candidate choosing this hopes the friction will disappear because it has been relabelled.

questions.explanation: Giving way on a smaller point to protect a larger one is a legitimate resolution, provided it is a deliberate trade made with the costs understood, rather than a reflex to avoid friction. The questions are what each side of the trade is worth, whether the concession can be recovered later, and whether the decision is within your own authority. Holding firm on a principle is not automatically stronger than yielding, if holding firm puts a bigger objective at risk.
questions.mindset: Know what you are trading when you give way, and give way only where the trade is worth it.

questions.stem: On a container terminal automation project, the crane-controls lead and the yard-systems lead agreed in a facilitated meeting two months ago that interface changes would be reviewed by the other team within two working days. Complaints have started again, each saying the other is ignoring the agreement. The agreement exists only in the notes you circulated after that meeting. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Meet both leads together to compare what was agreed with what has actually happened to the interface changes raised since the meeting.
options.rationale: Both say the other is breaking the agreement, so the first need is a shared view of the facts. Reviewing the actual changes against the commitment shows whether the agreement is being ignored, is unworkable, or is being read differently by each side.

options.text: Write to both leads restating the agreement they made, and ask each of them to confirm that they will keep to it from now on.
options.rationale: Restating the agreement assumes the problem is memory or willingness. A candidate choosing this has not asked why it is failing, and a reconfirmed agreement with the same flaw will fail again in the same way.

options.text: Escalate the renewed dispute to the sponsor, since a second breakdown shows the facilitated approach has not worked for these two leads.
options.rationale: This treats one relapse as proof that collaboration has failed. The dispute is about keeping an agreement nobody has been tracking, which the project manager can fix without spending the sponsor's attention.

options.text: Add the two-day review commitment to the project's interface management procedure, with turnaround tracked and reported at the weekly progress meeting.
options.rationale: An agreement that lives only in meeting notes has no owner and no measure, so each side can believe the other is breaking it. Building it into the procedure and reporting turnaround makes compliance visible and keeps it from decaying again.

options.text: Appoint a single integration coordinator to review all interface changes from both teams, so that neither lead depends on the other's turnaround.
options.rationale: This might be the right structure eventually, but it abandons the agreement before learning why it is failing and adds a role to work around two people. A candidate picking it has jumped to redesign without diagnosis.

questions.explanation: Reaching an agreement is only half of resolving a conflict; the other half is making sure it holds. Agreements that exist only in meeting notes tend to decay, because nobody measures them and each party remembers them differently. When a resolved conflict resurfaces, check the agreement against what has actually happened, then embed it in the project's normal procedures with a measure that makes compliance visible to both sides.
questions.mindset: A conflict is resolved when the agreement holds, not when it is reached.

questions.stem: Two developers on your video-streaming team were close friends until a falling-out outside work last month. Since then they have stopped speaking at stand-up, one walks out when the other presents at sprint reviews, and pairing sessions between them end early. Others on the team say they feel uncomfortable. Neither developer has raised anything with you. As the team's Scrum Master, which two actions should you take?

options.text: Bring the two of them together for a facilitated conversation to talk through the falling-out and agree how they can move past it.
options.rationale: Facilitated conversation is a standard conflict tool, which is why this is tempting. But the cause is a private matter outside work, and a Scrum Master has no standing to mediate a personal relationship that neither person has brought to them.

options.text: Speak privately to each of them about the specific behaviours seen at work and their effect on the team, without asking about the falling-out.
options.rationale: Walking out of reviews and silence at stand-up are workplace behaviours affecting the team, and addressing them is within the Scrum Master's remit. Keeping to what has been observed at work respects their privacy while making the expectation clear.

options.text: Raise the tension openly at the next retrospective, so that the whole team can say how the situation is affecting their work.
options.rationale: Openness is usually healthy in a retrospective, but this puts two people's private dispute in front of the team without their agreement. A candidate choosing it has confused team transparency with exposing individuals.

options.text: Agree with the team a temporary change to the pairing rotation so that the two are not paired together while things settle down.
options.rationale: Forced close contact is where the friction is costing the most, and a temporary rotation change is a team-level adjustment the Scrum Master can facilitate without singling anyone out. It reduces harm while the working relationship recovers.

options.text: Leave it for now, since neither of them has raised it and the cause lies outside work, and check again on how things are in a month.
options.rationale: Respecting privacy is right, but the behaviour is already affecting other team members. A candidate choosing this has treated the private origin of the conflict as a reason not to address its public effects.

questions.explanation: When a conflict starts outside work, the project manager's remit is its effect at work: the observable behaviour, the impact on others, and how the work is arranged. Addressing specific behaviour privately, and adjusting working arrangements to reduce friction, are within that remit; mediating the private relationship or exposing it to the team are not. Waiting because the cause is personal lets a private matter become the team's problem.
questions.mindset: Manage the behaviour you can see at work, and leave the private cause with the people who own it.

questions.stem: Your supplier team is building a grants management system for a government department using Scrum, inside the department's stage-gated programme. The programme office requires a weekly report showing percentage complete for each work package. Your team lead says this is meaningless for agile work and has stopped sending it, and the programme office has now escalated to your director. Which two actions should you take?

options.text: Instruct the team lead to resume the weekly report in the required format, because the programme office's reporting rules bind the supplier.
options.rationale: The rules may well bind the supplier, which makes this look safe. But it forces compliance without addressing the team lead's valid point, and the likely result is percentage figures nobody believes, which serves neither side.

options.text: Ask the programme office which decisions the percentage-complete figures feed, and what would happen if those decisions had to be made without them.
options.rationale: The programme office's position is a report format; its interest is the decisions the report supports, such as gate approvals and funding forecasts. Finding that interest opens options that satisfy it without inventing numbers.

options.text: Send the programme office a briefing on why percentage complete is not a valid measure for agile work, with the burn-up offered as a replacement.
options.rationale: This tells a customer that its need is wrong before understanding it. A candidate choosing it is arguing for the team's position rather than looking for what the programme office actually requires.

options.text: Work with the team lead to derive the figures the programme office needs from the release burn-up, with the method stated on the report.
options.rationale: Translating the team's real progress data into the form the programme office uses accepts the governance context while keeping the figures honest. Stating the method lets both sides trust what the numbers mean.

options.text: Ask your director to agree with the programme office that your team be exempted from the weekly report for the rest of the build.
options.rationale: An exemption ends the argument but leaves the programme office without what it needs for its gate decisions. A candidate choosing it is using escalation to win the position rather than resolve the conflict.

questions.explanation: Conflicts between delivery approaches usually show up as arguments about artefacts such as reports, documents and sign-offs. Underneath, each side has a legitimate interest: governance needs information to make decisions, and the team needs to report truthfully about how it works. The resolution is usually to identify the decision the artefact serves and supply that information in a form the work can honestly produce, rather than to make either side give in.
questions.mindset: Find the decision a report serves, and supply that in whatever form the work can honestly give.

questions.stem: A concert-ticketing product team is in conflict over the next release. In one-to-ones, three stakeholders told you more than their stated positions. Match each stated position to the interest that most likely sits underneath it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Head of marketing: 'The virtual queue must be live by 1 March.' She mentioned that a major spring tour goes on sale on 3 March.
Lead developer: 'We are not shipping the queue until the load test passes at 50,000 users.' He was on call when the site crashed during last year's festival sale.
Customer service manager: 'No release at all in March.' A third of her advisers are away on a training programme that month.

options.text: Having the queue working for a known high-demand on-sale date
options.rationale: The date matters because of the tour on-sale two days later. Seeing that, the team can explore what the queue must do by then, rather than arguing about the date itself.

options.text: Avoiding a repeat of a public failure under peak load
options.rationale: The specific load-test figure stands in for not reliving last year's crash. That interest might be met in other ways too, such as a capped queue or a staged rollout.

options.text: Having enough advisers available to handle customer questions after a change
options.rationale: The objection is to releasing when her team is short-staffed, not to releasing as such. Extra support cover or a release outside the training weeks could meet her interest.

options.text: Protecting the team's velocity figures ahead of a quarterly review
options.rationale: Not used. Nothing any stakeholder said points to velocity figures, and assuming a self-protective motive no one has expressed is the kind of attribution that hardens conflicts.

questions.explanation: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why they want it. Positions in a conflict are often incompatible while the interests behind them are not, so the useful work is to uncover the interests and look for options that satisfy them together. Listening for the reason behind each demand, especially the event or experience someone mentions alongside it, is how a deadlock over positions becomes a solvable problem.
questions.mindset: Ask why someone wants what they are demanding, because the answer is usually easier to satisfy than the demand.

questions.stem: On a predictive rollout of new tills across a bakery chain's 140 shops, three disagreements reach you on the same day. Match each one to when and how the project manager should step in. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two installation team leaders are giving one shop's staff contradictory instructions about whether to switch off the old tills at 14:00 or at 17:00 today.
In a weekly review attended by the client's retail director, your training lead sharply contradicts your deployment lead's account of why three shops went live late.
Two trainers disagree about whether to teach refunds before or after loyalty-card sales; both sequences are covered by the approved training plan.

options.text: Intervene straight away and give a single clear instruction
options.rationale: Shop staff are acting on conflicting orders today, so the harm is immediate and operational. Settling it is within the project manager's authority, and the reasons can be discussed with the two leaders afterwards.

options.text: Move the meeting on, then take it up privately with both leads straight afterwards
options.rationale: The disagreement is about facts that matter, but working it through in front of the client's director damages confidence and puts both leads on the defensive. It needs resolving today, just not in that room.

options.text: Leave it with the people involved and keep an eye on how it settles
options.rationale: Either sequence is within the approved plan, so nothing depends on the project manager deciding. Stepping in would take a choice away from the people best placed to make it.

options.text: Refer it to the project sponsor for a decision at the next steering meeting
options.rationale: Not used. None of the three needs the sponsor's authority: one needs action within the hour, one needs a private conversation, and one needs no intervention at all.

questions.explanation: Deciding when to step into a conflict depends on three questions: is harm happening now, who is watching, and does the matter need the project manager at all. Immediate operational harm calls for intervention on the spot; a disagreement on substance in front of an audience calls for deferral to a private setting the same day; and a disagreement within people's own discretion is often best left to them. Choosing the timing is as much a part of conflict management as choosing the approach.
questions.mindset: Decide when to step in before deciding how, and sometimes the answer is not at all.

questions.stem: You coach an agile team building a farm management app. Complete each sentence with the coaching response that fits the level the conflict has reached. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two developers disagree about the logging format. They share information openly and are both looking for the best answer, so the coach should
Team members now refer to 'the mobile camp' and 'the platform camp', bring up old defeats and lobby colleagues before meetings, so the coach should
One developer refuses to attend any meeting the other attends, says the other is acting in bad faith and wants them removed from the team, so the coach should

options.text: let the team work it through and observe without stepping in
options.rationale: A disagreement about a problem, conducted openly, is healthy conflict. Intervening would take a learning opportunity away from the team and signal that disagreement itself is a problem.

options.text: help both sides separate their interests from their positions and rebuild a shared set of facts
options.rationale: Camps, score-keeping and lobbying show the conflict has become a contest about winning. Bringing people back to interests and agreed facts is what moves it back towards problem-solving.

options.text: protect the people involved, separate them for now and bring in their managers or HR
options.rationale: When one party wants the other gone and attributes bad faith, the conflict has moved beyond what facilitation can fix. Protecting people comes first, and line management or HR have authority a coach lacks.

options.text: call a team vote so that the majority view settles the question
options.rationale: Not used. A vote creates winners and losers, so it would harden camps at the middle level and is no answer where people are at risk. Even at the lowest level the team does not need a vote imposed.

questions.explanation: Conflict escalates through recognisable levels, from a shared problem, through disagreement and contest, to a crusade or open hostility, and the right response changes with the level. At low levels the team should be left to resolve it; at middle levels the coach helps restore a focus on interests and facts; at the highest levels the priority is protecting people and involving those with formal authority. Applying a low-level response to a high-level conflict, or the reverse, makes it worse.
questions.mindset: Read how far a conflict has escalated before choosing how to respond to it.

questions.stem: Two leads on a veterinary diagnostics firm's hybrid programme disagree about which laboratory information system to buy. Before seeing any scores, they agreed these weights: data security 40%, five-year cost 25%, integration effort 20%, staff familiarity 15%. They then jointly scored each system from 1 to 5. System A scored 4, 2, 3 and 5; System B scored 3, 5, 4 and 2. Having seen the totals, the lead favouring System A proposes moving familiarity to 25% and cost to 15%. Work out the figures below.

blanks.label: Weighted score of System A under the agreed weights, to two decimal places
Weighted score of System B under the agreed weights, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: System B: 3 × 0.40 + 5 × 0.25 + 4 × 0.20 + 2 × 0.15 = 1.20 + 1.25 + 0.80 + 0.30 = 3.55, so B leads by 0.10 under the weights both leads agreed in advance.

blanks.label: Weighted score of System A under the proposed new weights, to two decimal places
blanks.rationale: With cost at 15% and familiarity at 25%: 4 × 0.40 + 2 × 0.15 + 3 × 0.20 + 5 × 0.25 = 1.60 + 0.30 + 0.60 + 1.25 = 3.75. System B falls to 3.25, so the proposal reverses the result.

blanks.label: Which system the method agreed before scoring selects (A or B)
blanks.rationale: Under the weights agreed before anyone saw the scores, System B wins at 3.55 against 3.45. The reweighting was proposed only after the totals were known, which is why it should not be adopted.

questions.explanation: Agreeing objective criteria and their weights before options are scored takes the personal element out of a disagreement, because both parties have committed to a method before knowing which answer it favours. That commitment only works if the method is protected afterwards: changing weights once the totals are visible reopens the conflict and turns the method into a tool for whoever is losing. A close result is a reason to look harder at the evidence, not to change the rules.
questions.mindset: Agree how a dispute will be decided before anyone knows which way the method points, then keep to it.

questions.stem: On a fintech app team, a tester asks you, as Scrum Master, to look over a message she plans to send a developer who keeps merging to the main branch without the review the team agreed. The diagram shows her draft, one sentence per box. Select the sentence most likely to escalate the conflict rather than resolve it.

graphic.title: A five-sentence draft message, one sentence per box
graphic.caption: Select a sentence. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: On three occasions this sprint, you merged to main without the one review our working agreement asks for.
regions.rationale: Pointing out a repeated breach can feel accusatory, which is why candidates pick it. But it is specific, checkable and tied to a rule the team wrote, so the developer can answer it without defending his character.

regions.label: Two of those merges broke the nightly build, and I spent most of Tuesday putting it right.
regions.rationale: Stating the cost can read as blame, but it describes a concrete consequence rather than a judgement. It is what tells the developer why the request matters, and it can be discussed on its facts.

regions.label: It is hard not to conclude that you think the team's rules do not apply to you.
regions.rationale: This moves from what he did to what he supposedly thinks of the team. An attributed motive cannot be discussed, only denied, so it invites him to defend his character instead of talking about the merges.

regions.label: I am frustrated by this, and I would like us to sort it out before the release.
regions.rationale: Candidates often assume that naming a feeling inflames things. Owning the feeling in the first person, alongside a wish to resolve it, is honest and gives the other person nothing to rebut.

regions.label: Could we agree that you wait for one approval before merging, even for small changes?
regions.rationale: A request can sound like a demand, which makes this tempting. But it is specific and answerable, and it offers a way forward that the developer can accept, discuss or counter.

questions.explanation: In a conflict conversation, the sentences that escalate are the ones that move from what someone did to who they are or what they intend. Observed behaviour, its concrete impact, the speaker's own feelings and a specific request can all be heard and answered; an attributed motive can only be denied, so the other person defends their character instead of discussing the behaviour. Coaching someone before a difficult conversation is largely helping them notice where description has slipped into interpretation.
questions.mindset: Describe what someone did and what it cost, and leave their motives out of it.
